newsitem.title: USA: Fed urged to enforce pay-to-play rules at banks.
newsitem.headline: Fed urged to enforce pay-to-play rules at banks.

text.p: Banks are facing fewer curbs by federal regulators on their sales of securities, including tax-exempt bonds, but that new freedom comes with a price, the MSRB will tell U.S. bank regulators.
The Municipal Securities Rulemaking Board will make the observations in a letter to bank regulators early next week, an MSRB official said.

The letter will remind regulators that as "firewalls" between bank holding companies and their muni securities departments gradually dissolve, more bank employees may be snared by the board's controversial "pay-to-play" rule, or G-37.
Enacted in April 1994, rule G-37 bars municipal dealers that make contributions to issuer clients from doing negotiated bond underwritings for two years with those governments.

"The firewalls are coming down," Christopher Taylor, MSRB's executive director, said in a telephone interview. "If a (bank employee) solicits muni securities business, by definition he is considered a municipal finance professional" covered by the rule, Taylor said.
And the bank must examine the contributions to see if it is banned from doing muni business with issuer, Taylor said.
Taylor said next week's letter will go to the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, Federal Reserve Board and Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation.
He said the board notified the American Bankers Association and Public Securities Association recently that it would send the letter.
Rule G-37 is "tough," Taylor said. "People ask why are you so tough. It's the American way of doing business. Well, not in this industry," he said, referring to the muni bond market.
